Tokyo,[a] officially the Tokyo Metropolis,[b] is the capital and most populous city of Japan. The population of the city proper was over 14 million as of 2023. The Greater Tokyo Area, which includes Tokyo and parts of six neighboring prefectures, is the third-most populous metropolitan area in the world, with 33 million residents as of 2025.[13]
Lying at the head of Tokyo Bay, Tokyo is part of the Kantō region, on the central coast of Honshu, Japan's largest island. It is Japan's economic center and the seat of the Japanese government and the Emperor of Japan. The Tokyo Metropolitan Government administers Tokyo's central 23 special wards, which formerly made up Tokyo City; various commuter towns and suburbs in its western area; and two outlying island chains, the Tokyo Islands. Although most of the world recognizes Tokyo as a city, since 1943 its governing structure has been more akin to that of a prefecture, with an accompanying Governor and Assembly taking precedence over the smaller municipal governments that make up the metropolis. Special wards in Tokyo include Chiyoda, the site of the National Diet Building and the Tokyo Imperial Palace; Shinjuku, the city's administrative center; and Shibuya, a hub of commerce and business.

Tokyo, originally known as Edo, rose to political prominence in 1603 when it became the seat of the Tokugawa shogunate, and by the mid-18th century, Edo had evolved from a small fishing village into one of the largest cities in the world, with a population surpassing one million. After the Meiji Restoration (1868), the imperial capital in Kyoto was moved to Edo, and the city was renamed Tokyo (lit. 'Eastern Capital'). Tokyo was greatly damaged by the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake and by Allied bombing raids during World War II. Beginning in the late 1940s, Tokyo underwent rapid reconstruction and expansion, which fueled the Japanese economic miracle, in which Japan's economy became the second-largest in the world at the time, behind that of the United States.[14] As of 2025, Tokyo is home to 26 of the world's 500 largest companies, as listed in the annual Fortune Global 500.[15]
Tokyo was the first city in Asia to host the Summer Olympics and Paralympics, in 1964, and also hosted in 2021. It hosted three G7 summits in 1979, 1986, and 1993. Tokyo is an international hub of research and development and an academic center, with several major universities, including the University of Tokyo, the top-ranking university in Japan.[16][17] Tokyo Station is the central hub for the Shinkansen, the country's high-speed railway network, and the city's Shinjuku Station is the world's busiest train station. Tokyo Skytree is the world's tallest tower.[18] The Tokyo Metro Ginza Line, which opened in 1927, is the oldest underground metro line in Asia.[19]

Title: Why Is Tokyo the Capital of Japan?

Japan is one of the most well-known countries in Asia. Millions of people from all around the world visit each year to experience Japan’s unique food, culture, architecture, and beautiful scenery. Among the wide range of distinctive must-see cities in Japan is the capital, Tokyo.
Tokyo is officially known as Tokyo Metropolis, and it has served as the capital of Japan since 1869. While typically referred to as a “city”, Tokyo is officially known and governed as a “metropolitan prefecture” as it is considered one of the 47 prefectures of Japan. This combination of city and prefecture is a characteristic unique to Tokyo.
Today, the Greater Tokyo Area is commonly recognized as the most populous metropolitan area in the world. But if you think Tokyo was picked as the capital of Japan based solely on its size, you’d be wrong. In fact, for eleven centuries, the capital of Japan was Kyoto. So why the change? Why is Tokyo the capital of Japan today?
_Take the quiz –__Can you name the 10 closest world capitals to Tokyo?_

## **The Capital of Japan**
Japan has actually had many capital cities throughout its long history. Traditionally, the national capital has always been the home of the Emperor. And from 794 through 1868, the Emperor lived in modern-day Kyoto. The site of Kyoto had been selected by Emperor Kanmu in the 8th century, as it was located away from an increasingly powerful and influential Buddhist clergy. Although future military rulers would sometimes establish their governments in other cities, Kyoto remained the seat of the Imperial Court until the 19th century.
Tokyo, on the other hand, was originally just a small fishing village called Edo. It very well might have remained just that, but in 1590, the military leader Tokugawa Ieyasu was reassigned to the Kantō region, and he made Edo his military headquarters. Tokugawa Ieyasu would work to assemble warriors and skilled craftsmen. He further fortified the city and surrounded the Edo Castle with moats and bridges. Soon, the original settlement of a hundred or so cottages was becoming a thriving city.
In 1603, Tokugawa Ieyasu was named shōgun, and he became the effective ruler of Japan. Edo continued to flourish, serving as _de facto_ national capital for the Tokugawa shogunate. Still, Japan’s imperial seat and official capital remained in Kyoto, but the Emperor was more or less powerless.

## **Why is Tokyo the Capital of Japan?**
The Tokugawa shogunate would usher in the longest period of peace and stability in the history of Japan, lasting over 260 years. However, by the mid-19th century, many in Japan were growing weary of an increasing Western influence on the nation, particularly in relation to the economy. In 1868, amidst the Boshin War, the Emperor and many powerful feudal lords were successful in overthrowing the shogunate.
The following year, 17-year-old Emperor Meiji moved to Edo, where the Tokugawa shogunate had previously ruled from. Under the Tokugawa shogunate, Edo had gradually become the nation’s political and cultural center. The city became the new official national capital once the Emperor came to town. Edo Castle became the new Imperial Palace, and the city of Edo was renamed Tokyo, meaning “Eastern Capital”.
The city of Tokyo was officially established on May 1, 1889. In 1943, the city of Tokyo merged with the prefecture of Tokyo and the Tokyo Metropolis was formed.

Learn about the long history of the capital city of Japan, from the early days in Kyoto and Edo to the development of Tokyo and its growth into a superpower.

## What is the capital city of Japan?
The capital city of Japan has changed throughout the many centuries of Japan’s history. In its earliest years, the emperor resided in Kyoto, in time the empire moved to Edo and eventually Tokyo was established. It is currently the capital of the country, and is the most populous prefecture (county) of Japan. Located at the head of Tokyo Bay, the prefecture forms part of the Kanto region. Tokyo is the political and economic centre of the country, the seat of the emperor and also where the national government operates.
Uncover the history of Tokyo with your class using this All About Tokyo PowerPoint.

## Geography of Tokyo
The metropolis of Tokyo is located in southern Kanto, is at the centre of a grand archipelago of islands and is bordered by the Edogawa River to the east and by mountains to the west. The city is split up into three major areas, the 23 ‘wards’ or districts of the city, the wider ‘tama’ area of greater Tokyo and the islands associated with Tokyo.

## Geography of Tokyo
#### 23-Special Ward Area
The 23-special ward area is the political, economic, and cultural hub of Japan. Government offices, corporations, and commercial facilities are concentrated in the heart of Tokyo, and the transportation network is well-developed.

## Geography of Tokyo
#### Tama Area
This area is highly urbanized and surrounds the 23 wards, but also has a beautiful natural environment including lakes, rivers, and green areas. Moreover, strong industrial capability and rich human resources made available through the concentration of universities, high-tech industries, and research institutes, make this area a region with high potential for the city of Tokyo.

## Geography of Tokyo
#### The Islands
This region has a rich natural environment abundant with marine resources, and the islands also play an important national role in securing a vast exclusive economic zone. They have a diverse and remarkable natural environment, as well as a unique historical and cultural background, and are precious assets providing valuable “healing” spaces for visitors.

## Geography of Tokyo
### Population of Toko
The population of Tokyo is estimated to be 13.491 million, or about 11% of Japan’s total population, and it has the largest population among all the 47 prefectures.
At 2,191 square kilometres, the area of Tokyo is 0.6% of the total area of Japan. With a population density of 6,158 persons per square kilometre, Tokyo is the most densely populated prefecture in Japan and one of the most densely populated cities in the word.
Create a fantastic classroom display all about the capital city of Japan with this Tokyo Display Poster Pack.

## History of the capital city of Japan
The development of Tokyo began in the 17th century, before that it was known as Edo and was the seat of the imperial palace in Japan. Its development say many ups and downs throughout the coming centuries before it would become the technological powerhouse of Japan, that it is today.

## History of the capital city of Japan
### Known as Edo
The history of the city of Tokyo stretches back over 400 years. It was originally named Edo, and was at first a simple fishing village. It began to grow and expand, eventually becoming a city. Its growth boomed when a military general, Tokugawa Leyasu, established the Tokugawa Shogunate in the city in 1603. Now at the centre of politics and culture in Japan, Edo grew into a huge city with a population of over a million people by the 1750s.
Throughout the Tokugawa Shogunate, the Emperor resided in Kyoto, which was the formal capital of the nation. When the Shogunate ended (bringing with it the end of the Edo Period), imperial rule was restored and the Emperor moved from Kyoto to Edo, which was then renamed Tokyo and officially became the capital of Japan.

## History of the capital city of Japan
### Opening up to the West
During the Meiji Era (1868-1912), Japan was opening up its culture to foreign trade and influence. The country began to assimilate much of western civilization into its own culture. Buildings of stone and brick were built on top of many of the mansions of feudal lords, the major roads were paved with cobbles and round stones. The first telecommunications line was opened in 1869 in Tokyo, and the first steam locomotive began running between Shimbashi and Yokohama in 1872. Tokyo was forever changed by this influence, and took on a different look to the traditional Japan city that it had previous been.
Even the people changed because of it, western hairstyles replaced the traditional topknot worn by men, and bowler hats, collared shirts and bustled skirts were the height of fashion.
Learn about one of the most famous sights in Japan, the evocative Mount Fuji, with this All About Mount Fuji PowerPoint.

## History of the capital city of Japan
### The Great Kanto Earthquake
During the Taisho era (1912-1926), there was a great migration into the cities, many people were able to find good jobs and improve their lives in places like Tokyo. Educational standards improved (for example, the number of girls going on to study at higher education increased rapidly).
Unfortunately, in September 1923, Tokyo was devastated by the Great Kanto Earthquake. The fires caused by the earthquake burned down much of the city centre. Over 140,000 people were reported as dead or missing and at least 300,000 buildings were destroyed.
After the earthquake, a reconstruction plan was formulated, but due to the high costs only a part of it was completed.

## History of the capital city of Japan
### The Effects of World War II
During the Showa era (1926-1989), the mood was low in Tokyo, rebuilding of the city had been slow, and the damage was widespread. Even so, the capital city of Japan opened its first subway line during this period.
The Pacific War, which broke out in 1941, would have an incredible impact on the city. The metropolitan administrative system was established and plans were put in place to prepare for attacks from the USA and her allies. During the final phases of the war, Tokyo was bombed over 100 times. The heaviest of these bombardments was an air raid in March 1945, in which thousands lost their lives.
When the war came to an end and Japan signed the ‘Instrument of Surrender’, much of Tokyo had been razed to the ground by the bombing and the population had fallen to half of what it was in 1940.

## History of the capital city of Japan
### Growth and Tokyo as we know it today
The 1950s were a time of gradual recovery for the nation of Japan, television broadcasting began in 1953 and Japan joined the United Nations in 1956. Advantages gained during the Korean War led to Japan entering a period of rapid economic growth in the 1960s. Due to technological innovations and new industries, this period saw mass production of everything from synthetic fibres to household electrical appliances.
During the 1970s, the previous economic growth began to show cracks, with increased pollution throughout the cities air and waterways, as well as noise pollution. In the 1980s, Japan was able to solve these problems and emerged into the world of Information Technology. Tokyo became one of the world’s most active major cities for cutting-edge technology, culture and fashion.
In the 21st century, Tokyo is seen as one of the most technologically advanced cities in the world, with huge skyscrapers and vast public transport networks.

Tokyo,[a] officially the Tokyo Metropolis,[b] is the capital and most populous city of Japan. The population of the city proper was over 14 million as of 2023. The Greater Tokyo Area, which includes Tokyo and parts of six neighboring prefectures, is the third-most populous metropolitan area in the world, with 33 million residents as of 2025.[13]
Lying at the head of Tokyo Bay, Tokyo is part of the Kantō region, on the central coast of Honshu, Japan's largest island. It is Japan's economic center and the seat of the Japanese government and the Emperor of Japan. The Tokyo Metropolitan Government administers Tokyo's central 23 special wards, which formerly made up Tokyo City; various commuter towns and suburbs in its western area; and two outlying island chains, the Tokyo Islands. Although most of the world recognizes Tokyo as a city, since 1943 its governing structure has been more akin to that of a prefecture, with an accompanying Governor and Assembly taking precedence over the smaller municipal governments that make up the metropolis. Special wards in Tokyo include Chiyoda, the site of the National Diet Building and the Tokyo Imperial Palace; Shinjuku, the city's administrative center; and Shibuya, a hub of commerce and business.

Tokyo, originally known as Edo, rose to political prominence in 1603 when it became the seat of the Tokugawa shogunate, and by the mid-18th century, Edo had evolved from a small fishing village into one of the largest cities in the world, with a population surpassing one million. After the Meiji Restoration (1868), the imperial capital in Kyoto was moved to Edo, and the city was renamed Tokyo (lit. 'Eastern Capital'). Tokyo was greatly damaged by the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake and by Allied bombing raids during World War II. Beginning in the late 1940s, Tokyo underwent rapid reconstruction and expansion, which fueled the Japanese economic miracle, in which Japan's economy became the second-largest in the world at the time, behind that of the United States.[14] As of 2025, Tokyo is home to 26 of the world's 500 largest companies, as listed in the annual Fortune Global 500.[15]
Tokyo was the first city in Asia to host the Summer Olympics and Paralympics, in 1964, and also hosted in 2021. It hosted three G7 summits in 1979, 1986, and 1993. Tokyo is an international hub of research and development and an academic center, with several major universities, including the University of Tokyo, the top-ranking university in Japan.[16][17] Tokyo Station is the central hub for the Shinkansen, the country's high-speed railway network, and the city's Shinjuku Station is the world's busiest train station. Tokyo Skytree is the world's tallest tower.[18] The Tokyo Metro Ginza Line, which opened in 1927, is the oldest underground metro line in Asia.[19]

## What is the capital city of Japan?
The capital city of Japan has changed throughout the many centuries of Japan’s history. In its earliest years, the emperor resided in Kyoto, in time the empire moved to Edo and eventually Tokyo was established. It is currently the capital of the country, and is the most populous prefecture (county) of Japan. Located at the head of Tokyo Bay, the prefecture forms part of the Kanto region. Tokyo is the political and economic centre of the country, the seat of the emperor and also where the national government operates.

## Geography of Tokyo
The metropolis of Tokyo is located in southern Kanto, is at the centre of a grand archipelago of islands and is bordered by the Edogawa River to the east and by mountains to the west. The city is split up into three major areas, the 23 ‘wards’ or districts of the city, the wider ‘tama’ area of greater Tokyo and the islands associated with Tokyo.

## Geography of Tokyo
#### 23-Special Ward Area
The 23-special ward area is the political, economic, and cultural hub of Japan. Government offices, corporations, and commercial facilities are concentrated in the heart of Tokyo, and the transportation network is well-developed.

## Geography of Tokyo
#### Tama Area
This area is highly urbanized and surrounds the 23 wards, but also has a beautiful natural environment including lakes, rivers, and green areas. Moreover, strong industrial capability and rich human resources made available through the concentration of universities, high-tech industries, and research institutes, make this area a region with high potential for the city of Tokyo.

#### The Islands
This region has a rich natural environment abundant with marine resources, and the islands also play an important national role in securing a vast exclusive economic zone. They have a diverse and remarkable natural environment, as well as a unique historical and cultural background, and are precious assets providing valuable “healing” spaces for visitors.

## History of the capital city of Japan
The development of Tokyo began in the 17th century, before that it was known as Edo and was the seat of the imperial palace in Japan. Its development say many ups and downs throughout the coming centuries before it would become the technological powerhouse of Japan, that it is today.

## History of the capital city of Japan
### Known as Edo
The history of the city of Tokyo stretches back over 400 years. It was originally named Edo, and was at first a simple fishing village. It began to grow and expand, eventually becoming a city. Its growth boomed when a military general, Tokugawa Leyasu, established the Tokugawa Shogunate in the city in 1603. Now at the centre of politics and culture in Japan, Edo grew into a huge city with a population of over a million people by the 1750s.
Throughout the Tokugawa Shogunate, the Emperor resided in Kyoto, which was the formal capital of the nation. When the Shogunate ended (bringing with it the end of the Edo Period), imperial rule was restored and the Emperor moved from Kyoto to Edo, which was then renamed Tokyo and officially became the capital of Japan.
texts.9:
## History of the capital city of Japan
### Opening up to the West
During the Meiji Era (1868-1912), Japan was opening up its culture to foreign trade and influence. The country began to assimilate much of western civilization into its own culture. Buildings of stone and brick were built on top of many of the mansions of feudal lords, the major roads were paved with cobbles and round stones. The first telecommunications line was opened in 1869 in Tokyo, and the first steam locomotive began running between Shimbashi and Yokohama in 1872. Tokyo was forever changed by this influence, and took on a different look to the traditional Japan city that it had previous been.
Even the people changed because of it, western hairstyles replaced the traditional topknot worn by men, and bowler hats, collared shirts and bustled skirts were the height of fashion.

texts.10:
## History of the capital city of Japan
### The Great Kanto Earthquake
During the Taisho era (1912-1926), there was a great migration into the cities, many people were able to find good jobs and improve their lives in places like Tokyo. Educational standards improved (for example, the number of girls going on to study at higher education increased rapidly).
Unfortunately, in September 1923, Tokyo was devastated by the Great Kanto Earthquake. The fires caused by the earthquake burned down much of the city centre. Over 140,000 people were reported as dead or missing and at least 300,000 buildings were destroyed.
After the earthquake, a reconstruction plan was formulated, but due to the high costs only a part of it was completed.
texts.11:
## History of the capital city of Japan
### The Effects of World War II
During the Showa era (1926-1989), the mood was low in Tokyo, rebuilding of the city had been slow, and the damage was widespread. Even so, the capital city of Japan opened its first subway line during this period.
The Pacific War, which broke out in 1941, would have an incredible impact on the city. The metropolitan administrative system was established and plans were put in place to prepare for attacks from the USA and her allies. During the final phases of the war, Tokyo was bombed over 100 times. The heaviest of these bombardments was an air raid in March 1945, in which thousands lost their lives.
When the war came to an end and Japan signed the ‘Instrument of Surrender’, much of Tokyo had been razed to the ground by the bombing and the population had fallen to half of what it was in 1940.
texts.12:
## History of the capital city of Japan
### Growth and Tokyo as we know it today
The 1950s were a time of gradual recovery for the nation of Japan, television broadcasting began in 1953 and Japan joined the United Nations in 1956. Advantages gained during the Korean War led to Japan entering a period of rapid economic growth in the 1960s. Due to technological innovations and new industries, this period saw mass production of everything from synthetic fibres to household electrical appliances.
During the 1970s, the previous economic growth began to show cracks, with increased pollution throughout the cities air and waterways, as well as noise pollution. In the 1980s, Japan was able to solve these problems and emerged into the world of Information Technology. Tokyo became one of the world’s most active major cities for cutting-edge technology, culture and fashion.
In the 21st century, Tokyo is seen as one of the most technologically advanced cities in the world, with huge skyscrapers and vast public transport networks.

Transcriptions

Tokyo was originally known as Edo (江戸), a kanji compound of 江 (e, 'cove, inlet') and 戸 (to, 'entrance, gate, door').[26] The name, which can be translated as "estuary", is a reference to the original settlement's location at the meeting of the Sumida River and Tokyo Bay. During the Meiji Restoration in 1868, the name of the city was changed to Tokyo (東京; from 東 tō 'east', and 京 kyō 'capital'), when it became the new imperial capital,[27] in line with the East Asian tradition of including the word for capital (京) in the name of the capital city (for example, Kyoto (京都), Keijō (京城), Beijing (北京), Nanjing (南京), and Xijing (西京)).[26] During the early Meiji period, the city was sometimes called Tōkei, an alternative pronunciation for the same characters representing "Tokyo", making it a kanji homograph. Some surviving official English documents use the spelling "Tokei";[28] however, this pronunciation is now obsolete.[29]

This essay provides a brief introduction to the history of a place at 35.6762° North, 139.6503° East. Exactly, Tōkyō. The following guide offers a comprehensive explanation of the transformation the city undertook from the decline of Edo onwards. The ascent of imperial Tōkyō is briefly depicted in the mirror of the introduction of Western architecture (1), the evolution of the inner-city transport system (2) and the organization of the urban space (3). Thus, the birth of the modern world capital Tōkyō is laid out for the contemporary visitor that is keen to discover the history and evolution of the urban heritage of this modern world capital ready for staging the 2020 Olympic Games.
**Focus on Japanese Cities**
Research regarding Edo and Tōkyō is extremely extensive: For centuries, urban research in architecture, anthropology, sociology, geography, Japanese Studies and even humanities like philology and arts have produced an abundant amount of literature on this city. This interest is predominantly fueled by the extraordinary development of urban Japan. As early as in sixteenth century Japanese cities had gained a paramount importance over rural Japan — even if in the mirror of a Japanese hinterland becoming increasingly accessible to Western research recent regional studies picked up momentum. To be fair it is mainly the wealth of Japan’s economy and culture that made academics as well as the general public interested in the exploration of Japan’s urban culture. And by sheer number alone the megacity Tōkyō has become one of the most important global hubs since the beginning of the Meiji period. Especially since the economic growth in the post-war period made large part of the financial flows cross the city. Many more strategic decisions affecting people far beyond the Pacific region are made here. No wonder academics around the world have an interest in exploring the various aspects of this city:

In German-speaking countries, this interest is shared by various researchers and institutes.[[1]](https://medium.com/@hamp.mathias/from-edo-to-tokyo-birth-of-a-global-capital-c9effafada34#_ftn1) First to mention are the activities of the Duisburg Institute for East Asian Studies. Back in the 1960s, Peter Schöller’s exploration of Japan’s urban spaces had inspired a whole generation of young scientists, among whom: Winfried Flüchter for urban planning and land reclamation and the research on urban planning by Uta Hohn and Carola Hein are important contributions. In French, among others, Augustin Berque offers a remarkable account of architectural theory. There is also Nicolas Fiévé’s work on urban history and Phillipe Pons on urban sociology. Among the abundant English contributions are for instance William Coaldrake on power structure, Henri Smith II on architectural theory, and for urban and architectural history David Stewart, Edward Seidensticker, Roman Cybrinsky, Kenneth Frampton, James Hoare. Jinnai Hidenobu, Dōmon Fuyuji, Hasegawa Takashi, Fujita Hiroo, Muramatsu Shin and Fujimori Terunobu are among the many Japanese city historians who pay particular attention to the history, practice, law, demography and planning culture of Japanese urban development.

## 1 Tokyo before Meiji, 1457–1868
As already mentioned above, Tōkyō before the ascent of Imperial Japan throughout the Meiji time was called Edo.[**[2]**](https://medium.com/@hamp.mathias/from-edo-to-tokyo-birth-of-a-global-capital-c9effafada34#_ftn2) For centuries this castle town near the river delta of Eastern Kantō was the destination of annual processions (_sankin kōtai_). These pilgrimages occurred throughout the year from all over Japan to pay respect to the Tokugawa Shoguns and their followers. Edo was only renamed Tōkyō after the Restauration of the Imperial household with Emperor Meiji Mutsuhito as house herald in 1868. [[3]](https://medium.com/@hamp.mathias/from-edo-to-tokyo-birth-of-a-global-capital-c9effafada34#_ftn3) Edo’s story can be divided into the following periods:
**1.1 City Foundation, 1457–1602**
The city founding of today’s Tōkyōs goes back to Ōta Dōkan (1432–1486). This samurai was a military tactician and Buddhist monk turned poet who declared a strategically located fishing village in the center of the Kantō plain as his seat of rule. The first castle complex he built near the banks of a river called Sumidagawa is considered to be the origin of Edo. Throughout the years a modest castle town (_jōkamachi_) developed around this rudimentary castle complex. In late sixteenth century Edo was taken under the rule of the Tokugawa gaining its importance as shogunal capital and political center of Japan only after the victory of Tokugawa Ieyasu in the Battle of Sekigahara in 1603.
**1.2 Edo and the Tokugawa, 1603–1853**

## 1 Tokyo before Meiji, 1457–1868
Under the rule of the thirteen consecutive Tokugawa-Shoguns Edo knew a hitherto unprecedented population growth, even exceeding that of London and Paris at times.[[4]](https://medium.com/@hamp.mathias/from-edo-to-tokyo-birth-of-a-global-capital-c9effafada34#_ftn4) During the Edo period, which lasted from 1603 to 1868, various areas of the city experienced heydays and less glorious days. Except the recurring destruction to fire outbreaks, it is above all the social division of Edo that can be considered the most characteristic aspect of Edo during this epoch. The division was aimed at underlining the hierarchical structure of Tokugawa society in urban space. This resulted in divided quarters for samurai, peasants, artisans and traders (_shinōkōshō_) according to the feudal estates-based societal rules (_mibun seido_).[[5]](https://medium.com/@hamp.mathias/from-edo-to-tokyo-birth-of-a-global-capital-c9effafada34#_ftn5)
Edo organized the urban space in following parts: a castle area (1), adjacent _buke-chi_, that is districts for feudal heirs called _daimyo_(2), various temple and shrine areas _tera-machi_ or even _monzen-machi_ (3), and space for commoners (4). Tokugawa rule assigned common citizens only a narrow space at east of the castle town on the banks of Sumidagawa river and the shoreline to Edo bay (today: Tōkyō Bay). There far below the castle (_shitamachi_) a city of its own developed. Mainly for traders and craftsmen the lower city showed an incredible density. In midst of countless water channels, which drew their water partly from Sumidagawa, partly from neighboring rivers and cut through all quarters, the culture of the common people (_chōnin bunka_) with their special high places (_meisho_) developed. The urban cultural of these days consisted of entertainment districts, markets and teahouses and became the meeting place of the pleasurable Edo citizen. A Minamoto member of the Imperial Court, Minamoto no Yoritomo, broke away from the court in 1180. At Kamakura, south of Edo, he set up Japan's first shogunate, a feudal lord system of governance that followed a warrior code. One of his vassals was Edo Shigenaga, Shigetsugu's son. Shigenaga was rewarded by the shogunate with patches of land around Edo, including the village Kitami. In 1185, the Minamoto defeated the Taira.[2][13][14][15] A road from Kamakura to Edo, and the Kozuke-Fuchu road, were used by armed bands on their way to fight battles in the Middle Ages.[2]
Kamakura and Muromachi periods (1185–1573)edit  
Further information: Kamakura period and Muromachi period
After 1185, a Minamoto branch that settled in Kozuke would eventually become the Tokugawa clan, who ruled Edo from the 17th to the 19th centuries.[2]
Around 1439, the Uesugi clan in Kanto was made up of two families: the Yamanouchi and Ogigayatsu, who switched been being allies or enemies. The Yamaouchi gained control of the Kanto governor who lived in Kamakura, and the Ogigayatsu supported them. Ōta Dōkan was appointed in 1455 as a vassal to the Ogigayatsu head Sadamasa, who served Kyoto's Ashikaga shogunate. Sadamasa commissioned him to build camp-like "castles" across the Musashi plain. In 1456, entering Edo, the Edo family still living there left, avoiding a fight with the Uesugi. They moved to their property in Kitami, giving their land and castle to Dōkan.[15][16][17][18]
Ōta Dokan, who built the start to Edo Castle

Edo Castle began construction in 1457 at the modern Imperial Palace's East Garden. It was west of the Edo village, at the Chiyoda peasant village. The castle was in a strategic spot, as it was defensible and near the multiple rivers' estuaries. Boats could anchor near the castle.[16][19][20] The Chiyoda peasants were moved away for construction. At the time, the castle was more of a square camp with "earthen embankments" featuring landscaping projects, fences, a few buildings, and wells.[16] Shrines and temples were built nearby, and the dock turned into a center for Chinese goods.[19][20] The name Chiyoda was later given to an area in Tokyo's center.[16]
After 1458, Dōkan stayed in the Edo region, conquered the plain, and gained a correspondence with the emperor. At the time, the villages of Hibiya, Iigura, Iwaida, Mita, Sakurada, Shiba and Takarada were present. The suffixes ta or da in Japanese place names implies rice cultivation. At some point, Dōkan had the Hachiman shrine built on the Ichigaya hill. A second shrine was built next to Hachiman, likely honoring his family, as their mon (emblem), the kikyo flower, is present. In the late 15th century, the Yamanouchi and Ogigayatsu fought. Dōkan was loyal to Sadamasa, but Sadamasa was suspicious and jealous of him. In 1486, Sadamasa invited Dōkan to his house and murdered him. Dōkan's tomb is in the Doshoin temple near Mount Oyama. He is considered Edo's founder, and there are multiple monuments to him at Tokyo City Hall and the Imperial Palace.[16][17] The Ōta clan survived as minor nobles for 300 years after.[15]
Later historyedit

The plains were not safe for travelers. The bandit Owada Dogen gained a dangerous reputation there. However, villagers in Shibuya likely had sympathy for him, as he was a fugitive from a 1526 battle that ended the Shibuya clan. A hill was named Dōgenzaka after him, which is now a street in Shibuya.[13][21]
The Uesugi conflict led to the Hojo clan gaining power in Kanto. In 1524, at Kawagoe, Hojo Oitsuna fought against Uesugi Tomo, and captured Edo Castle. The castle later belonged to the Koga family's Ashikaga Shigeuji, and then the Hojo again. The Hojo's representative at Edo was Toyama Kaganao. In 1563, Ōta Dōkan's great-grandson failed an attempt to recapture the castle. For a long time, the castle stayed Hojo property.[16]
Azuchi-Momoyama period (1568–1600)edit  
Further information: Azuchi–Momoyama period  
Tokugawa Ieyasu, who made Edo the capital of his shogunate.

From 1560 to 1582, Oda Nobunaga's army overthrew the Ashikaga Shogunate, and unified half of the country.[22] He did not seem to have interest in Edo. Nobunaga's successor, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, continued Nobunaga's conquests. Hideyoshi and his army's commander, the Tokugawa Ieyasu, took control of the Hojo in 1589.[23] Hideyoshi unexpectedly gave Ieyasu the gift of Hojo territories in Kanto as a fief, if Ieyasu gave him his territories in the south. This was an attempt to neutralize Ieyasu as a potential threat by moving him away from Kyoto. In 1590,[24][25][26] Ieyasu visiting Edo was considered crucial to the city's legitimacy.[26] In 1598, after Hideyoshi died, there was struggle to be shogun between Ieyasu and Hideyoshi's vassals. Ieyasu won at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600. Ieyasu started building a new government's capital in Edo. He dictated the social structure Mansfield calls "the most well-managed feudal society the world has ever known".[23][25][27]
Tokugawa period, 1600–1700edit  
Main article: Tokugawa shogunate  
Further information: Edo period and Edo society
The Tokugawa period began when the Imperial Court appointed Ieyasu shōgun in 1603, starting the Tokugawa shogunate.[23] Japan's imperial seat and official capital remained in Kyoto, but the Emperor was virtually powerless; Ieyasu was the effective ruler of Japan, and Edo became powerful as the capital.[20][28][29]

Tokyo,[a] officially the Tokyo Metropolis,[b] is the capital and most populous city of Japan. The population of the city proper was over 14 million as of 2023. The Greater Tokyo Area, which includes Tokyo and parts of six neighboring prefectures, is the third-most populous metropolitan area in the world, with 33 million residents as of 2025.[13]
Lying at the head of Tokyo Bay, Tokyo is part of the Kantō region, on the central coast of Honshu, Japan's largest island. It is Japan's economic center and the seat of the Japanese government and the Emperor of Japan. The Tokyo Metropolitan Government administers Tokyo's central 23 special wards, which formerly made up Tokyo City; various commuter towns and suburbs in its western area; and two outlying island chains, the Tokyo Islands. Although most of the world recognizes Tokyo as a city, since 1943 its governing structure has been more akin to that of a prefecture, with an accompanying Governor and Assembly taking precedence over the smaller municipal governments that make up the metropolis. Special wards in Tokyo include Chiyoda, the site of the National Diet Building and the Tokyo Imperial Palace; Shinjuku, the city's administrative center; and Shibuya, a hub of commerce and business.
texts.3:
Tokyo, originally known as Edo, rose to political prominence in 1603 when it became the seat of the Tokugawa shogunate, and by the mid-18th century, Edo had evolved from a small fishing village into one of the largest cities in the world, with a population surpassing one million. After the Meiji Restoration (1868), the imperial capital in Kyoto was moved to Edo, and the city was renamed Tokyo (lit. 'Eastern Capital'). Tokyo was greatly damaged by the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake and by Allied bombing raids during World War II. Beginning in the late 1940s, Tokyo underwent rapid reconstruction and expansion, which fueled the Japanese economic miracle, in which Japan's economy became the second-largest in the world at the time, behind that of the United States.[14] As of 2025, Tokyo is home to 26 of the world's 500 largest companies, as listed in the annual Fortune Global 500.[15]
Tokyo was the first city in Asia to host the Summer Olympics and Paralympics, in 1964, and also hosted in 2021. It hosted three G7 summits in 1979, 1986, and 1993. Tokyo is an international hub of research and development and an academic center, with several major universities, including the University of Tokyo, the top-ranking university in Japan.[16][17] Tokyo Station is the central hub for the Shinkansen, the country's high-speed railway network, and the city's Shinjuku Station is the world's busiest train station. Tokyo Skytree is the world's tallest tower.[18] The Tokyo Metro Ginza Line, which opened in 1927, is the oldest underground metro line in Asia.[19]

Tokyo's nominal gross domestic output was 120.2 trillion yen (US$887.9 billion) in FY2022 and accounted for 21.2% of Japan's economic output, which converts to 8.43 million yen or US$62,291 per capita.[20] Including the Greater Tokyo Area, Tokyo is the second-largest metropolitan economy in the world after New York, with a 2022 gross metropolitan product estimated at US$2.08 trillion.[21] Although Tokyo's status as a leading global financial hub has diminished with the Lost Decades since the 1990s, when the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) was the world's largest, with a market capitalization about 1.5 times that of the NYSE,[22] Tokyo is still a leading financial hub, and the TSE remains among the world's top five major stock exchanges.[23] Tokyo is categorized as an Alpha+ city by the Globalization and World Cities Research Network. It ranked 14th in the 2024 edition of the Global Livability Ranking,[24] and has been ranked as the safest city in the world by the Economist Intelligence Unit.[25]

As already mentioned above, Tōkyō before the ascent of Imperial Japan throughout the Meiji time was called Edo.[**[2]**](https://medium.com/@hamp.mathias/from-edo-to-tokyo-birth-of-a-global-capital-c9effafada34#_ftn2) For centuries this castle town near the river delta of Eastern Kantō was the destination of annual processions (_sankin kōtai_). These pilgrimages occurred throughout the year from all over Japan to pay respect to the Tokugawa Shoguns and their followers. Edo was only renamed Tōkyō after the Restauration of the Imperial household with Emperor Meiji Mutsuhito as house herald in 1868. [[3]](https://medium.com/@hamp.mathias/from-edo-to-tokyo-birth-of-a-global-capital-c9effafada34#_ftn3) Edo’s story can be divided into the following periods:
**1.1 City Foundation, 1457–1602**
The city founding of today’s Tōkyōs goes back to Ōta Dōkan (1432–1486). This samurai was a military tactician and Buddhist monk turned poet who declared a strategically located fishing village in the center of the Kantō plain as his seat of rule. The first castle complex he built near the banks of a river called Sumidagawa is considered to be the origin of Edo. Throughout the years a modest castle town (_jōkamachi_) developed around this rudimentary castle complex. In late sixteenth century Edo was taken under the rule of the Tokugawa gaining its importance as shogunal capital and political center of Japan only after the victory of Tokugawa Ieyasu in the Battle of Sekigahara in 1603.

## 1 Tokyo before Meiji, 1457–1868
Under the rule of the thirteen consecutive Tokugawa-Shoguns Edo knew a hitherto unprecedented population growth, even exceeding that of London and Paris at times.[[4]](https://medium.com/@hamp.mathias/from-edo-to-tokyo-birth-of-a-global-capital-c9effafada34#_ftn4) During the Edo period, which lasted from 1603 to 1868, various areas of the city experienced heydays and less glorious days. Except the recurring destruction to fire outbreaks, it is above all the social division of Edo that can be considered the most characteristic aspect of Edo during this epoch. The division was aimed at underlining the hierarchical structure of Tokugawa society in urban space. This resulted in divided quarters for samurai, peasants, artisans and traders (_shinōkōshō_) according to the feudal estates-based societal rules (_mibun seido_).[[5]](https://medium.com/@hamp.mathias/from-edo-to-tokyo-birth-of-a-global-capital-c9effafada34#_ftn5)
Edo organized the urban space in following parts: a castle area (1), adjacent _buke-chi_, that is districts for feudal heirs called _daimyo_(2), various temple and shrine areas _tera-machi_ or even _monzen-machi_ (3), and space for commoners (4). Tokugawa rule assigned common citizens only a narrow space at east of the castle town on the banks of Sumidagawa river and the shoreline to Edo bay (today: Tōkyō Bay). There far below the castle (_shitamachi_) a city of its own developed. Mainly for traders and craftsmen the lower city showed an incredible density. In midst of countless water channels, which drew their water partly from Sumidagawa, partly from neighboring rivers and cut through all quarters, the culture of the common people (_chōnin bunka_) with their special high places (_meisho_) developed. The urban cultural of these days consisted of entertainment districts, markets and teahouses and became the meeting place of the pleasurable Edo citizen. A Minamoto member of the Imperial Court, Minamoto no Yoritomo, broke away from the court in 1180. At Kamakura, south of Edo, he set up Japan's first shogunate, a feudal lord system of governance that followed a warrior code. One of his vassals was Edo Shigenaga, Shigetsugu's son. Shigenaga was rewarded by the shogunate with patches of land around Edo, including the village Kitami. In 1185, the Minamoto defeated the Taira.[2][13][14][15] A road from Kamakura to Edo, and the Kozuke-Fuchu road, were used by armed bands on their way to fight battles in the Middle Ages.[2]
Kamakura and Muromachi periods (1185–1573)edit  
Further information: Kamakura period and Muromachi period
After 1185, a Minamoto branch that settled in Kozuke would eventually become the Tokugawa clan, who ruled Edo from the 17th to the 19th centuries.[2]
Around 1439, the Uesugi clan in Kanto was made up of two families: the Yamanouchi and Ogigayatsu, who switched been being allies or enemies. The Yamaouchi gained control of the Kanto governor who lived in Kamakura, and the Ogigayatsu supported them. Ōta Dōkan was appointed in 1455 as a vassal to the Ogigayatsu head Sadamasa, who served Kyoto's Ashikaga shogunate. Sadamasa commissioned him to build camp-like "castles" across the Musashi plain. In 1456, entering Edo, the Edo family still living there left, avoiding a fight with the Uesugi. They moved to their property in Kitami, giving their land and castle to Dōkan.[15][16][17][18]

Edo Castle began construction in 1457 at the modern Imperial Palace's East Garden. It was west of the Edo village, at the Chiyoda peasant village. The castle was in a strategic spot, as it was defensible and near the multiple rivers' estuaries. Boats could anchor near the castle.[16][19][20] The Chiyoda peasants were moved away for construction. At the time, the castle was more of a square camp with "earthen embankments" featuring landscaping projects, fences, a few buildings, and wells.[16] Shrines and temples were built nearby, and the dock turned into a center for Chinese goods.[19][20] The name Chiyoda was later given to an area in Tokyo's center.[16]
After 1458, Dōkan stayed in the Edo region, conquered the plain, and gained a correspondence with the emperor. At the time, the villages of Hibiya, Iigura, Iwaida, Mita, Sakurada, Shiba and Takarada were present. The suffixes ta or da in Japanese place names implies rice cultivation. At some point, Dōkan had the Hachiman shrine built on the Ichigaya hill. A second shrine was built next to Hachiman, likely honoring his family, as their mon (emblem), the kikyo flower, is present. In the late 15th century, the Yamanouchi and Ogigayatsu fought. Dōkan was loyal to Sadamasa, but Sadamasa was suspicious and jealous of him. In 1486, Sadamasa invited Dōkan to his house and murdered him. Dōkan's tomb is in the Doshoin temple near Mount Oyama. He is considered Edo's founder, and there are multiple monuments to him at Tokyo City Hall and the Imperial Palace.[16][17] The Ōta clan survived as minor nobles for 300 years after.[15]

The plains were not safe for travelers. The bandit Owada Dogen gained a dangerous reputation there. However, villagers in Shibuya likely had sympathy for him, as he was a fugitive from a 1526 battle that ended the Shibuya clan. A hill was named Dōgenzaka after him, which is now a street in Shibuya.[13][21]
The Uesugi conflict led to the Hojo clan gaining power in Kanto. In 1524, at Kawagoe, Hojo Oitsuna fought against Uesugi Tomo, and captured Edo Castle. The castle later belonged to the Koga family's Ashikaga Shigeuji, and then the Hojo again. The Hojo's representative at Edo was Toyama Kaganao. In 1563, Ōta Dōkan's great-grandson failed an attempt to recapture the castle. For a long time, the castle stayed Hojo property.[16]
Azuchi-Momoyama period (1568–1600)edit

From 1560 to 1582, Oda Nobunaga's army overthrew the Ashikaga Shogunate, and unified half of the country.[22] He did not seem to have interest in Edo. Nobunaga's successor, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, continued Nobunaga's conquests. Hideyoshi and his army's commander, the Tokugawa Ieyasu, took control of the Hojo in 1589.[23] Hideyoshi unexpectedly gave Ieyasu the gift of Hojo territories in Kanto as a fief, if Ieyasu gave him his territories in the south. This was an attempt to neutralize Ieyasu as a potential threat by moving him away from Kyoto. In 1590,[24][25][26] Ieyasu visiting Edo was considered crucial to the city's legitimacy.[26] In 1598, after Hideyoshi died, there was struggle to be shogun between Ieyasu and Hideyoshi's vassals. Ieyasu won at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600. Ieyasu started building a new government's capital in Edo. He dictated the social structure Mansfield calls "the most well-managed feudal society the world has ever known".[23][25][27]
Tokugawa period, 1600–1700edit  
Main article: Tokugawa shogunate  
Further information: Edo period and Edo society
The Tokugawa period began when the Imperial Court appointed Ieyasu shōgun in 1603, starting the Tokugawa shogunate.[23] Japan's imperial seat and official capital remained in Kyoto, but the Emperor was virtually powerless; Ieyasu was the effective ruler of Japan, and Edo became powerful as the capital.[20][28][29]
